questions.prompt: Reading a[0], then a[1], then a[2] is mainly an example of
options: Spatial locality
A pipeline hazard
Thrashing
An interrupt
questions.explanation: Nearby addresses are used close together. Temporal locality would be reading the same address again soon.

questions.prompt: Which are the three classic cache-miss reasons?
options: Compulsory: this block has not been requested yet
Capacity: the working set does not fit
Conflict: the wanted block maps to a set that is already full
Ethical: the program has not been reviewed
questions.explanation: Every miss is a first touch, a capacity problem, or a mapping collision. The names are compulsory, capacity, and conflict.

questions.prompt: A direct-mapped cache has 8 lines and one word per block. Address 19 maps to which line if line = address mod 8?
questions.explanation: 19 = 2 × 8 + 3, so the line index is 3 and the tag is 2.
traps: Keeping the quotient (the tag) and throwing away the remainder.

options: Updates the line and marks it dirty; memory is written when the line is evicted
Writes memory on every store and never keeps a dirty bit
Ignores stores
Clears the cache after each instruction
questions.explanation: Write-through updates memory on the store. Write-back waits, which saves traffic and needs a dirty bit so the eviction is not lost.
traps: Swapping the names write-back and write-through.

questions.prompt: In the simple model hit time + miss rate × miss penalty, average memory access time grows when
options: The miss rate or the miss penalty grows
Hit time shrinks and nothing else changes
The program stops touching memory
The word size becomes one byte, with no other change to the formula
questions.explanation: The second term is the extra time you pay on misses. Raising either factor raises the average.

questions.prompt: Making cache blocks larger, and changing nothing else, usually
options: Captures spatial locality, but moves more data on a miss
Removes the need for a tag
Turns every access into a hit
Makes the cache the same size as main memory
questions.explanation: A bigger block brings in neighbors the program may use next. The cost is a larger miss penalty and fewer blocks for the same capacity.

questions.prompt: Raising a cache from direct-mapped to 2-way set associative, at the same capacity, mainly cuts
options: Conflict misses
Compulsory misses on the first touch of a block
The number of bits in an address
Disk seek time
questions.explanation: A set with two ways gives a block a second place to live, so two hot blocks that share an index can coexist. The first touch of a block is still compulsory.
traps: Associativity does not erase the first-touch miss.

questions.prompt: Direct-mapped, 4 lines, one word per line, initially empty. Accesses: 0, 4, 0. How many misses?
questions.explanation: 0 misses into line 0. 4 maps to the same line and replaces it, a second miss. 0 is no longer present, so the third access misses too.
traps: Calling the third access a hit because “0 was seen earlier”, after 4 has evicted it.

questions.prompt: A cache is much smaller than RAM. Why does it still speed up ordinary programs?
questions.answer: Programs reuse a small set of addresses and the addresses next to them, so a small fast store captures most accesses.
questions.explanation: Temporal locality rewards keeping a recently used block. Spatial locality rewards bringing its neighbors along. That is the whole bet.
